name: The Testing Effect
statement: Retrieving a fact from memory fixes it better than reading it again.
meaning: The act of retrieving information from memory — testing yourself — strengthens long-term retention more than spending the same time restudying the material. A test is not merely a measurement of what you know; the effort of recall itself changes memory and improves later recall. Practising retrieval beats rereading for making learning last.
mechanism: Several overlapping accounts are offered, and the mechanism is not settled. Retrieval is a desirable difficulty: a hard but successful recall benefits memory more than an easy re-exposure. Elaborative retrieval holds that pulling a fact from memory elaborates its traces and cue-target links. The multiple-routes account holds that each retrieval adds another path back to the stored memory. And practising the very act of recall the final test will demand — transfer-appropriate processing — improves performance on it. Retrieval reinstates and updates the context in which the material was learned, binding it more richly.

examples.text: Roediger and Karpicke had students study science passages then either reread or take a recall test with no feedback; rereading won after five minutes, but testing won decisively after two days and a week, roughly preventing several days of forgetting.

In a follow-up, a group that read a passage about three times and tested repeatedly recalled more after a week than a group that read it some fourteen times and never tested — retrieval beating sheer re-exposure.
Self-quizzing, practice exams, and flashcards are everyday forms of retrieval practice, turning testing from assessment into a tool for learning.

variants.name: Retrieval with feedback
variants.text: Adding feedback to a test typically strengthens the effect further, especially by correcting errors before they consolidate — important where initial recall is likely to fail.

variants.name: Retrieval practice for transfer
variants.text: Karpicke and Blunt's finding that retrieval practice produced more learning than elaborative study with concept mapping, including on inference questions — though transfer to novel contexts is more contested.

whyItMatters: It overturns the intuition that tests only measure learning by showing that they cause it, one of the most practically important results in the science of study. It explains why rereading, which feels productive, is among the weaker strategies, and why self-testing, which feels harder, is among the strongest — a lesson with direct force for how students and teachers should spend their time.

working.text: practise recalling material from memory rather than rereading it, since retrieval builds far more durable retention.
check your answers after retrieving, especially for material you are likely to get wrong, to correct errors before they set.
prefer the effortful feeling of self-testing over the easy fluency of rereading, which flatters without teaching.

limits: It is among the more replicated findings in cognitive psychology, confirmed by large meta-analyses, but it has boundary conditions. It works best when the initial test permits reasonably high success and comes relatively soon after learning, and feedback matters most where initial recall is weak. Some researchers argue the benefit can shrink for very complex, interconnected material, a live debate, with the practical fix of building understanding first and testing after. Transfer of the benefit to genuinely novel questions is more contested than the same-material effect. And much foundational work rests on undergraduate samples.
misreadings: A test is not only an assessment — it is itself a learning event, the central correction this research makes. Rereading is not the best way to study; it produces fluency and confidence but comparatively weak long-term retention, and its ease misleads. And the effect is not mere re-exposure: restudy groups re-experience all of the material, yet still lose to testing at a delay, so it is the retrieval, not the second look, that does the work.
origin: Noted in outline by Francis Bacon and William James, and studied experimentally from the early twentieth century; established in its modern form by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke's 'Test-Enhanced Learning' (Psychological Science, 2006), with robustness confirmed by later meta-analyses.

sources.text: Roediger & Karpicke, "Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention," Psychological Science 17(3):249-255 (2006). — the prose-passage experiments and the delayed-test crossover.

Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan, "Rethinking the Use of Tests: A Meta-Analysis of Practice Testing," Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701 (2017). — practice testing outperforming restudy across 118 articles.
Karpicke & Blunt, "Retrieval Practice Produces More Learning than Elaborative Studying with Concept Mapping," Science 331(6018):772-775 (2011). — retrieval practice and transfer.
